extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary critics, advanced readers and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for writing and critically reading the modern novel — how to construct a novel (selection, arrangement, point of view, scene vs picture, characterization, etc.) and how a critic/reader should reconstruct and judge the book's craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form / shape of the book
rubrics_metrics.description: A book has a certain form or shape which can be ascribable to it (good or bad) and is an essential aspect of the novel as an object of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism must attempt to perceive the book’s overall form even though it is revealed progressively and is hard to retain in memory; treat the novel as a rounded object and ask whether its form functions to express the subject. Anti-pattern: treating the novel solely as 'life' and failing to notice its formal outline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading aright / creative reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning of criticism is to read aright — to get into touch with the book and to recreate the novel’s form in the reader’s mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic/reader must actively recreate the book (a 'creative reader' or 'novelist' in the act of reading), holding the novel slightly at a distance to perceive its design, rather than becoming lost in the illusion of the story. Practice and deliberate effort are required; passive immersion is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist’s making consists crucially in selection (choosing what to lift from life) and arrangement (distributing the material in a single design).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how the author has selected, discarded, and ordered material: has he/she thrown aside accidental material and concentrated on what is meaningful? The critic should examine how selection and arrangement serve the subject. Example: Tolstoy lifts fragments and completes them into an ordered design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism / truth and vividness (likeness to life)
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel should 'realize' life — be true, vivid, convincing and like life where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readers’ common gift to 'realize' scenes and judge whether the representation is true to human experience. But recognize that literal transcript is impossible and that truth may be achieved through artful shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization / command of life
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful command of character and the knowledge of human affections and manners is a primary quality; memorable people endure in the reader’s memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters have been rendered with consistent depth, whether their presence persists after reading, and whether the author’s imagination has given them life. Anti-pattern: characters that are memorable only as isolated scenes but not integrated into the book’s form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, design, composition (laws of art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form, design, and composition (borrowed from other arts) are applicable to the novel and contribute to its quality even if they fit imperfectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider proportion, balance, and how parts cohere into a whole. But be realistic: a novel may succeed despite imperfect construction; weigh form against life and other virtues rather than applying dogmatic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of metaphors from the visual arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'colour', 'perspective', 'composition' are metaphors imported from material arts and cannot be pressed too literally when applied to literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such metaphors as hints and suggestions for method, but be cautious: the novel is a temporal, processual art and cannot be measured as a painting or statue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative modes / forms of narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: There are various narrative forms (dramatic, pictorial, scenic, generalized, panoramic, etc.), each with different properties and uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which modes the novelist employs and evaluate whether each is properly used where its peculiar strength is required. The critic should learn to recognize and name these modes through conscious reading of exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama (scene) vs. picture (panoramic / general survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene (dramatic incident) and the picture (panoramic/general survey) are distinct modes: scene shows events acted in full; picture covers longer time/space with economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes for culminating, demonstrative moments where full visibility is needed; use picture for breadth and accumulated impressions. Anti-patterns: overusing dramatization where economy would serve better (wasting scene), or neglecting fully wrought scenes that clinch effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of time and space
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic scenes are 'expensive' in time/space; oblique/narrative summary can render long periods more economically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the author has economized appropriately: did a scene need to be dramatized in full, or could a brief narrative have preserved pace and proportion? Scenes should be prepared and not forced to bear undue burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and placement of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene should be prepared in advance; a fully wrought scene functions best when it clinches effects prepared by earlier material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether scenes are placed so they gather and resolve prior issues; avoid scenes that are isolated, unprepared, or merely indulged without structural necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / narrative perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The point of view gives the general 'look' or attitude of the book and is a fundamental decision shaping treatment and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the selected viewpoint suits the subject and whether the author maintains or manipulates it coherently. The choice of perspective affects what details can be shown and how inner life is mediated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intermediary consciousness (subject-centred narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling a story through somebody’s consciousness (interposed mind) can turn a pictorial, thin report into something dramatized and powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the interposition of a mind (narrator or focalizer) enhances clarity and dramatic reality rather than merely distancing the reader from events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and coherence (building impressions into structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The impressions received while reading must be marshalled and concentrated into a coherent, appraisable structure — a 'welded mass'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the reader can reconstruct the whole as a unified design; ask whether disparate scenes and pictures combine logically to express the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: The subject as primary determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist’s choice of subject — the fruitful idea — is the cardinal gift and determines the appropriate treatment and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the treatment arises naturally from the subject, whether the author started from the 'heart' of the subject, and whether deviations weaken expression. If the subject is poor, even good craft may falter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical literacy about narrative 'substances'
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and writers must learn the properties of the 'different substances' of a novel (the various modes of narrative) and how to use them aright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should be able to recognize and handle scene, incident dramatized/pictured, panoramic impression, generalized narrative, etc., as distinct materials with distinct capacities and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader as co-creator (reader responsibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader (especially the critical reader) must accept a share of responsibility in making the book by recreating and fashioning it from its impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active, constructive reading is required: stand above the material, avoid purely receptive watching and instead shape the novel in the mind to perceive its form. Passive reading leads to loss of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding critical shyness and preserving pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should not be inhibited by a scruple that dissecting a novel destroys its life; the pleasure of creation (recreating craft) may exceed the pleasure of illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not avoid analysis for fear of spoiling enjoyment; dissecting art is legitimate and necessary for understanding craft, though care should be taken not to be needlessly destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy and proper conjunction of modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different narrative modes have relative values and should be used in proper conjunction: e.g., the scene often serves as final stroke while picture accumulates impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a writer combines modes across the progress of the story; observe where drama should be subordinated or where picture must prepare a later scene. The critic can seek inductive generalizations by comparing many novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and distribution of emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must manage the pacing — how much time and emphasis each part receives, ensuring that the weight of dramatization and description aligns with the story’s needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for wasted passages, over-lengthy scenes, or insufficient build-up. The best uses of dramatic moments are when they crown effects already half-made — pacing should enable scenes to act swiftly and sharply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of method weaknesses into strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherent weaknesses of some methods (e.g., thinness of pictorial report) can be acknowledged and turned into distinctive strengths (e.g., focusing on the mind-as-mirror).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author has deliberately emphasized the method's limitations to produce a new, valuable effect (e.g., interior focalization dramatized by the mind's reflections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of critical vocabulary / need for technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism is hampered by an unsettled vocabulary for narrative modes; critics should aim to define and use terms with technical acceptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to develop clear names and delimitations for types of narrative (e.g., dramatic, pictorial, scenic, generalized) and apply them precisely when analyzing craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of critical certainty (memory problems, imprecision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism faces inherent limits: imperfect memory and the difficulty of describing a temporal art in literal, unequivocal terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge uncertainty in judgments; aim to approach and approximate the book’s making rather than claim absolute exactness. Use close study and repeated reading to reduce fallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of dramatization to clinch matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama (fully rendered scenes) is best used to 'clinch' matters — to demonstrate results and crown effects prepared by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether dramatized moments serve as decisive confirmations of developments rather than gratuitous display. Anti-pattern: using drama as filler or habitually breaking into dialogue without structural gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern for workmanship / critic as craftsman
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must be a craftsman who knows how to handle the material that forms in his mind while reading and to recognize its fine variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate technical familiarity and practical habits of analysis; without workmanship the critic cannot construct a coherent recreated book. Anti-pattern: relying purely on impressionistic praise without attending to method.
